extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, media scholars, and readers interested in public opinion and the press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining the standards, constraints, and evaluative criteria by which newspapers select, frame, and report news versus the standards of truth and organized intelligence that should inform public understanding. Focuses on editorial practice, source reliability, newsworthiness, and institutional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish news from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: News and truth are not the same thing: 'The function of news is to signalize an event, the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts, to set them into relation with each other, and make a picture of reality on which men can act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where social conditions take measurable shape do news and truth coincide; reporters should not treat news items as full statements of truth. Be explicit about the difference between a signal/event and a verified, contextualized truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report source reliability (avoid overstating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are responsible for judging the reliability of sources and must not make an event appear more certain than the source warrants (example: do not print 'Lenin Dead' when only an unreliable source says so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When information is from an uncertain source, head it and present it as such (e.g., 'Helsingfors says Lenin is dead'). The paper should avoid repeating uncertain claims as established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness tied to reader impact and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to be presented as interference with the reader's life because attention is provoked by personal identification; editors select and play up items that will absorb readers' limited attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To interest readers quickly, present stories through familiar footholds and stereotypes that let the reader identify personally with the situation (e.g., emphasize inconvenience from strikes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection shaped by stereotypes and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions and stereotypes (e.g., labeling a group a 'combine' vs 'leading business men') cue readers' reactions and are central to how newspapers frame events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such labels shape public feeling and can bias presentation; reporters/editors should be conscious of how word choices predispose reader judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt acts get reported; underlying causes often omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reporters and readers lack direct experience of complex, underlying processes (e.g., causes of strikes), news is usually an account of overt phases (demands, strikes, disorder) rather than the deeper reasons behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must make extra effort (and are constrained) to surface causes; otherwise the public will see only the stereotyped event. Editors should avoid letting the story be only the reader's inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reportability depends on measurable, recorded events
rubrics_metrics.description: The news is precise in proportion to the precision with which the event is recorded; unless an event can be named, measured, and given shape, it either fails to be news or is subject to observation accidents and prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer items with clear record or measurable attributes; when dealing with unrecorded matters, indicate uncertainty and avoid pretending precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic, temporal, and legal constraints shape coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadlines, fixed page size, competition for minutes, space limits, libel law risk, and the need to interest the buying public force editors into systematization and routine judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that these constraints justify standardization but also create blind spots; where feasible allocate space/effort to complex stories despite the pressure to simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of reporting chaos and remote events
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaos (wars, revolutions) is hardest to report; when access is limited, reporting is produced by censors, propagandists, or distant intermediaries, producing evocative but stereotyped accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of accounts produced where direct access is impossible; seek multiple perspectives and disclose limits of access to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press influence spreads via exemplars and wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain newspapers (often with resources to buy cables) take a lead in reporting a subject, their form becomes a model for others; reporting practice often flows from centers of access and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the tendency to import frames from dominant outlets (e.g., London correspondence) and actively question whether the adopted model fits local realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must judge probable reader interest, not only ethical perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors select items, positions, and prominence based on what will absorb a given set of readers' attention, not solely on ethical or religious perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is partly a business judgment; ethical aims must be balanced with the practical need to engage readers, but editors should be aware when commerce unduly distorts civic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers create and reinforce opinion through framing and editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to create opinion resides in the combination of news selection, stereotypes, and editorial reinforcement; editorials can give readers a clue to engage with confusing news and help shape identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorials responsibly to clarify rather than to manipulate; disclose framing devices and provide context to reduce undue partisanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Once readership partisanship is evoked, editorial change is difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: If a newspaper has mobilized readers' partisanship on an issue, even an editor convinced of a needed change will find it hard to shift position without delicate management; often issues are allowed to taper off instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage transitions carefully; prefer transparent gradual shifts and explain reasons rather than simply letting coverage vanish to avoid backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited body of exact knowledge constrains journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: There is only a small body of exact recorded knowledge (e.g., public records) that requires no special training; beyond that journalists operate largely in discretion because social facts lack authoritative canons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where domain knowledge exists, rely on verifiable records; where it does not, acknowledge the subjective construction of 'truth' and invite expert input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press quality is an index of social organization and institutional record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The better institutions record and represent interests and introduce objective criteria, the more affairs can be presented as news; poor institutional recording produces sensational or misleading news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for better records, audits, and institutional transparency to improve the factual basis of reporting; treat press improvement as linked to institutional reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press cannot substitute for organized intelligence and social science
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is too frail to carry the whole burden of popular sovereignty or to supply all knowledge democrats expect; social scientists and organized intelligence (audits, statistics) are needed to produce usable formulations of social facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage development and use of systematic social data, expert reports, and comparable records to feed the press; journalists should work with specialists to improve public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should convey the uncertain character of many social 'truths'
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can and should bring home to people the uncertainty of the truths on which opinions are founded and prod the development of more usable social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on contested or poorly recorded matters, explicitly communicate uncertainty and range of interpretations; avoid presenting one-sided conclusions as settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting often privileges easily recordable incidents over complex but important truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many deeper truths (standards of living, productivity, human rights) are endlessly debatable without exact records, routine news will favor sensational or stereotyped facts over subtle analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make space for explanatory journalism and efforts to gather quantitative evidence; resist the tendency to reduce complex social issues to mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of organized, comparative records for creating experimental social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When experiences (school districts, factories, health departments, etc.) are recorded and available for comparison, the number of comparable experiences approaches genuine experiment and improves public decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote standardized record-keeping and comparability across jurisdictions and institutions so journalists and social scientists can report and test policies more reliably.
